newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea suspected as defector shot near Seoul.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea suspected as defector shot near Seoul.

text.p: Two gunmen shot and seriously wounded a North Korean defector near the South Korean capital Seoul, and a senior police officer said the attack appeared to have been ordered by the communist North.
The attack, late on Saturday, came as China agonised over what to do about a high North Korean offical now holed up in the South Korean mission in Beijing and seeking asylum in the South.

The South Korean police officer told Reuters he suspected North Korean agents carried out the shooting to send Seoul a stark warning over the latest defection attempt by Hwang Jang-yop, a member of the secretariat of Pyongyang's ruling Workers' Party.

"We don"t have any proof at the moment but we suspect North Korea ordered the men to carry out the attack to warn the South after Hwang Jang-yop's defection," said the officer, who asked not to be identified.
He said a full-scale manhunt was under way for the gunmen.
Police identified the injured man as Li Il-nam (known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong). They said he had defected in the early 1980s via Europe where he had been studying.

Li, 36, was the first North Korean defector to be shot in the South since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War, according to police. They said he was the nephew of a girlfriend of North Korea's top leader Kim Jong-il.

Tensions on the divided peninsula, always high, soared after Hwang arrived by taxi on Wednesday at Seoul's diplomatic mission in the Chinese capital. South Korea says he sought asylum, while North Korea insists he was kidnapped.
Analysts in Beijing said China was unlikely to make a decision on Hwang's fate until after North Korea celebrated Kim Jong-il's 55th birthday on Sunday.

Li, 36, was shot in the head and chest outside his temporary home at Bundang, just south of Seoul, late on Saturday, they said. A nurse at a nearby hospital said the defector later underwent surgery but he remained unconscious.

Police believed the attackers used silencers as neighbours heard no gunshots, another police officer said. An analysis of two used cartridges at the scene showed the weapons used were Belgian-made handguns.
Hwang's apparent betrayal has caused a massive loss of face for a North Korean government already reeling from severe food shortages and economic disasters.
He ranked 24th in the Stalinist state's hierarchy and would be the most senior of its officials to seek asylum in the South.
China must decide whether to allow him to be flown to Seoul, where he could be expected to reveal crucial secrets about the North Korean state, or to send him back to Pyongyang.
Hwang, the scholarly architect of North Korea's national ideology of Juche, or self-reliance, was reported to be adamant that he wanted to go to South Korea and nowhere else.
"I will die here if my determination to go to South Korea cannot be realised," he said in a statement released by Seoul authorities.

Beijing has appealed for calm while it investigates and South Korea appeared to accept this approach after a meeting between its Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Singapore.
"I think we have started a good discussion with China and we have to wait and see," Yoo said on Saturday. "I don't think that it's right now to make any judgment on this."
Fearing retaliation, even before Saturday's shooting, South Korea had ordered tighter security at all its overseas missions.
Despite the 1953 truce, the two Koreas have remained implacable foes. Their tense border, bristling with advanced weapons, is today the last Cold War frontier.
